titleStmt.author: Rosellina Ferraro
James R. Bettman

publicationStmt.p: Tag layer of the DHSS Meta-Tagging Project. The article text is reproduced from the staged copy named in sourceDesc and is not altered; the tags are held separately in standOff so that overlapping and nested spans are preserved.

bibl.title: The Power of Strangers: The Effect of Incidental Consumer Brand Encounters on Brand Choice

person.p: the tag layer; a sentence written by the tagger about the paper, always anchored to a quotation but not itself a quotation

span.label: mechanism
span.quote: Four studies provide evidence that repeated exposure to simulated ICBEs increases choice of the focal brand for people not aware of the brand exposure, that perceptual fluency underlies these effects, and that these effects are moderated by perceivers’ automatic responses to the type of user observed with the brand.

span.label: incidental consumer brand encounters
span.quote: We refer to these situations as incidental consumer brand encounters (ICBEs).

span.label: behavioural-experiment
span.quote: We simulated ICBEs by briefly exposing participants to photos of people engaged in everyday situations (e.g., sitting on a bench, having lunch).

span.label: Only a single brand (Dasani) was used, so effects of competing-brand clutter are untested.
span.note: what this limits: the transfer to a real shelf: OUR RESEARCH UTILIZED ONLY ONE BRAND, WHEREAS IN THE REAL WORLD PEOPLE DO NOT JUST ENCOUNTER ONE BRAND
span.quote: For example, our research utilized only one brand, whereas in the real world people do not just encounter one brand.

span.label: The stimuli were static photographs, not the dynamic encounters people actually have.
span.note: what this limits: the ecological reading of the exposure: OUR PHOTOGRAPHS PRESENT A STATIC PICTURE OF AN ICBE, not the dynamic encounters people actually have
span.quote: Our photographs present a static picture of an ICBE.

span.label: Participants who were aware of the brand exposure were too few to analyse, so the aware case is untested.
span.note: what this limits: the scope of the whole finding: WE FOCUS ONLY ON THE RESULTS FOR THE UNAWARE PARTICIPANTS ... AS THERE ARE TOO FEW PARTICIPANTS IN THE AWARE GROUP FOR MEANINGFUL ANALYSES - the aware/unaware contrast is untested
span.quote: We focus only on the results for the unaware participants below as there are too few participants in the aware group for meaningful analyses.

span.label: The authors concede an alternative explanation for study 4 in terms of analytic vs. holistic processing styles tied to self-construal.
span.note: what this limits: the study 4 interpretation: SOME READERS MAY WONDER IF PROCESSING STYLE DIFFERENCES ASSOCIATED WITH DIFFERENT SELF-CONSTRUALS PROVIDE AN ALTERNATIVE EXPLANATION - conceded, not excluded
span.quote: Some readers may wonder if processing style differences associated with different self-construals provide an alternative explanation for our study 4 results.

span.label: fluency
span.quote: Study 2 shows that, if the experienced fluency generated by repeated exposure can be attributed to another source, then the effect will be attenuated

span.label: type of user
span.quote: When a type of user is discernible, however, this relationship is moderated by perceivers’ automatic responses to that group

span.label: mere exposure
span.quote: Our results go beyond an interesting application of mere exposure by showing that the context in which repeated exposure occurs matters

span.label: brand choice
span.quote: This research examines how ICBEs influence brand choice. Four studies provide evidence that repeated exposure to simulated ICBEs increases choice of the focal brand

span.label: THE MECHANISM IS PROVED BY MISATTRIBUTION, WHICH IS THE STRONGEST FORM AVAILABLE FOR A FEELING: `Study 2 shows that, IF THE EXPERIENCED FLUENCY generated by repeated exposure CAN BE ATTRIBUTED TO ANOTHER SOURCE, then the effect WILL BE ATTENUATED.` Give the ease somewhere else to have come from and the preference goes with it. **That rules out the alternative that repetition simply builds a memory or a habit** - a memory would not care where you thought the ease came from
span.quote: Study 2 shows that, if the experienced fluency generated by repeated exposure can be attributed to another source, then the effect will be attenuated

span.label: AND THE DOSE-RESPONSE IS NON-MONOTONIC: `Study 3 suggests that TOO MUCH FLUENCY CAN BACKFIRE, which is consistent with the SATURATION MODEL.` More exposure is not more effect. **This is the one finding here that a replication is most likely to invert by accident**: increasing the number of exposures to be safe would move the design past the peak and find less. A corpus that records `repeated exposure increases choice` without the saturation clause would license exactly that mistake
span.quote: Study 3 suggests that too much fluency can backfire, which is consistent with the saturation model proposed by Fazendeiro et al

span.label: UNAWARENESS USED AS A CONTROL RATHER THAN REPORTED AS A FINDING: `the participants in study 4 WERE NOT AWARE of the brand and hence COULD NOT BE AWARE of its association with the in-group or out-group, SO CONSCIOUS CORRECTION WAS NOT POSSIBLE.` **This is higgins1977's discounting cue turned into a design feature.** Higgins found that noticing your own bias ATTENUATES it; here, showing that participants could not notice is what licenses reading the result as uncorrected. Same mechanism, opposite use - one paper measures it, the other rules it out by construction
span.quote: Importantly, the participants in study 4 were not aware of the brand and hence could not be aware of its association with the in-group or out-group, so conscious correction was not possible

span.label: AN ANOMALY REPORTED AGAINST THEIR OWN ACCOUNT, IN THEIR OWN DISCUSSION: `While we found a positive increasing correlation between liking and choice of Dasani with increased exposure, REPORTED LIKING ITSELF DID NOT DIFFER ACROSS CONDITIONS. On the surface, this result seems INCONSISTENT WITH A FLUENCY ACCOUNT.` The exposure moved what people CHOSE without moving what they SAID they liked. **A measure and its supposed cause coming apart** - and the authors raise it themselves, under a heading of its own, rather than leaving it in a table
span.quote: While we found a positive increasing correlation between liking and choice of Dasani with increased exposure, reported liking itself did not differ across conditions

span.label: builds-on → Winkielman et al. (2003)
span.quote: Our findings are in line with the assertions of Winkielman et al. (2003) that effects of fluency can be attenuated when other relevant information is available and utilized.

span.label: builds-on → Fazendeiro et al. (2007) and Huber and O’Reilly (2003) saturation model
span.quote: Study 3 suggests that too much fluency can backfire, which is consistent with the saturation model proposed by Fazendeiro et al. (2007) and Huber and O’Reilly (2003).

span.label: replicates → Fang et al. (2007)
span.quote: The results for this condition were similar to those of the fluency misattribution case, which is consistent with the Fang et al. (2007) results.

span.label: contradicts → Simonson, Kramer, and Young (2004)
span.quote: Additionally, evidence in Simonson, Kramer, and Young (2004) suggests that effects on preference ratings are usually larger than effects on choice.

span.label: fluency —causes→ brand choice
span.note: direction on the measure: increases · strength of the relation: 0.9 — THE PAPER'S CENTRAL CLAIM, and the axis quote carries the awareness qualifier that the abstract attaches to it - `for people NOT AWARE of the brand exposure`. Weight 0.9 rather than 0.95 because the relation is non-monotonic (study 3) and moderated (study 4), and an unqualified `fluency increases choice` is true only in the middle of the range.
span.quote: This research examines how ICBEs influence brand choice. Four studies provide evidence that repeated exposure to simulated ICBEs increases choice of the focal brand for people not aware of the brand exposure, that perceptual fluency underlies these effects

span.label: type of user —causes→ fluency
span.note: strength of the relation: 0.85 — THE MODERATOR, AND NO `effect_direction` - DELIBERATELY. The paper says the type of user can `BOLSTER it ... DAMPEN it ... or OVERPOWER it` depending on the group and the perceiver's construal, so there is no single sign. A `causes(increases)` here would be false a third of the time. The vocabulary offers no `moderates`, and this is the nearest honest use of what it has.
span.quote: This suggests that implicitly discerning the type of user of a brand may moderate the fluency effect arising from increased frequency of exposure

span.quote: f group (i.e., 0 p out-group, 1 p in-group), and the value of construal at one standard deviation below the mean (4A), at the mean (4B), and at one standard deviation above the mean (4C

span.label: regression
span.quote: A logistic regression was used to analyze the data, with the dependent variable coded as 1 p chose Dasani or 0 p did not choose Dasani.

span.label: standard-deviation
span.quote: type of group (i.e., 0 p out-group, 1 p in-group), and the value of construal at one standard deviation below the mean (4A), at the mean (4B), and at one standard deviation above the mean (4C
